The Home Depot · UX MEOW

UX MEOW: a place to practice design leadership.

I co-founded UX MEOW to connect interns, designer mentors, and innovation opportunities. The program gave teams real problems to explore and designers a supported way to practice mentoring and leadership.

Role
Staff UX Designer · program co-founder and mentor trainer
Scope
Project sourcing, mentor training, and a guided team sprint
Key decision
Support mentors with a guided sprint, check-ins, and shared feedback
Outcome
Six to 16 project teams; three participants accepted full-time UX-team roles

I — Inspiration

Connect three needs through one program

OrangeWorks Engineering sometimes lacked real projects for summer interns. Innovation ideas waited for resources. UX designers wanted opportunities to develop their mentoring skills.

A fellow Staff Designer approached me about creating mentor training. Together, we developed UX MEOW: designer-led teams that paired interns with mentors to explore real innovation opportunities. Interns gained practical experience, mentors practiced small-group leadership, and project champions had a team to help develop their ideas.

D — Design Process

Give mentors and teams a shared starting point

I developed mentor training materials, led workshops, and sourced projects. My co-founder and I worked with innovation champions to turn their ideas into practical starting points. The training addressed a specific leadership habit: mentors needed to invite uncertainty, rather than wait for someone to volunteer that they were stuck.

We built a guided collaboration board around the GV design sprint process, with activity instructions and supporting resources. The first cohort brought 12 interns and 12 designer mentors together in six teams. An unpacking day introduced research, technical constraints, stakeholder interview transcripts, and experts so teams could understand the opportunity before proposing solutions.

Make it easier to say where the work is stuck

We taught mentors to go beyond “Does anyone need help?” and prompt each person about their work. My program partners and I modeled that practice by joining check-ins, listening, and asking questions.

E — Engagement

Make feedback part of the work

Teams developed problem statements, explored alternatives through Crazy 8s and sketches, and built low-fidelity prototypes. At the midpoint, they presented the opportunity, business goals, and design decisions to champions and stakeholders.

That review gave teams a chance to explain their reasoning and respond to feedback. They revised prototypes, coded solutions, and tested with Home Depot customers and employees. The work produced working explorations and field tests; it did not establish production launches.

A — Action

Help the program carry forward

I co-founded and helped run UX MEOW from 2019 through my departure in 2022. We adapted it for remote work in 2020, and returning mentors helped train others and update the materials.

The program expanded across engineering, UX, and product management, then opened to employees interested in technical roles. Its structure gave participants a way to build experience while contributing to a real project.

S — Success

From six teams to a broader opportunity

6 → 16
Project teams as UX MEOW expanded
3
Participants who accepted full-time UX-team roles

Reported program outcomes. The first cohort had 12 interns and 12 designer mentors across six teams.

UX MEOW grew from six to 16 project teams. Three participants from non-technical backgrounds applied for and accepted full-time UX-team positions. These were shared program outcomes, supported by my co-founder, mentors, project champions, and the teams involved.

My takeaway: leadership development needs a place to practice. MEOW combined real work, guidance, and feedback so participants could contribute while developing the skills to lead others.
